title: A red ball bounces on green ground

steps.text: Select **$root**, the top node of your scene.
steps.why: New nodes are added under whatever is selected.

steps.text: Click **+**, search for `StaticBody3D`, and press **Create**. This will be the ground.
steps.why: A StaticBody3D never moves, but other bodies collide with it.

steps.text: With **$ground** selected, add a `MeshInstance3D` as its child.
steps.why: A physics body draws nothing; a MeshInstance3D is what you see.

steps.text: In the Inspector, click **<empty>** next to **Mesh** and choose **New PlaneMesh**.
Click the new **PlaneMesh** to open it, and set **Size** to x `20`, y `20`.
steps.why: A bigger plane gives the ball room to land.

steps.text: Set **Geometry ▸ Material Override** to **New StandardMaterial3D**.
steps.why: A material decides how a surface looks: its colour, shine and so on.

steps.text: Open the material and set **Albedo ▸ Color** to green.
steps.why: Albedo is the surface's base colour.

steps.text: Select **$ground** again and add a `CollisionShape3D` as its child.
steps.why: The mesh is only how it looks. The collision shape is what the ball actually hits.

steps.text: Set its **Shape** to **New WorldBoundaryShape3D**.
steps.why: A world boundary is an endless flat floor, so the ball can't miss it.

steps.text: Select **$root** again and add a `RigidBody3D`. This will be the ball.
steps.why: A RigidBody3D is moved by physics: gravity pulls it down and it bounces off what it hits.

steps.text: Set **$ball**'s **Position** (under Transform) to x `0`, y `10`, z `0`.
steps.why: Y is up in Godot 3D, so the ball starts 10 metres above the ground.

steps.text: With **$ball** selected, add a `MeshInstance3D` as its child.
Set its **Mesh** to **New SphereMesh**.
Set **Geometry ▸ Material Override** to **New StandardMaterial3D**.
Open the material and set **Albedo ▸ Color** to red.
Select **$ball** again and add a `CollisionShape3D` as its child.
Set its **Shape** to **New SphereShape3D**.
steps.why: The sphere shape is the same size as the sphere mesh, so what you see is what collides.

steps.text: Select **$ball** and set **Physics Material Override** to **New PhysicsMaterial**.
steps.why: A physics material decides how a body feels: how bouncy and how slippery.

steps.text: Open the physics material and set **Bounce** to `0.8`.
steps.why: 0 doesn't bounce at all, 1 bounces back to the same height. 0.8 loses a little each time.

steps.text: Select **$root** and add a `Camera3D`.
steps.why: A 3D game shows the world through a camera. Without one you'd see nothing.

steps.text: Set the camera's **Position** to x `0`, y `4`, z `12`.
steps.why: This puts it back and a little up, looking at the ground and the ball.

steps.text: Select **$root** and add a `DirectionalLight3D`.
steps.why: A directional light is like the sun. Without light the game would be dark.

steps.text: Set the light's **Rotation** to x `-50`, y `30`, z `0`, so it shines down at an angle.
steps.why: A light pointing straight ahead would barely light the ground.

steps.text: Press **F6** (Play the currently edited scene) and watch the red ball drop onto the green ground and bounce. Close the game window when you're done.
steps.why: F6 runs just this scene. Godot saves your work first.
